items: Recognize that your toddler's aggression is reactive, not intentional - their prefrontal cortex is only 5% developed, so they literally cannot control impulses before acting.
Stop asking 'why did you do that?' because your toddler genuinely doesn't know the answer - their brain didn't give them a 'why' option before the behavior happened.
Replace 'no hitting' commands with positive behavior statements like 'Hands are gentle' because toddlers process the word 'hitting' more than the negation in the command.
Remember that your toddler isn't giving you a hard time - they are having a hard time, which means the aggression is neurological rather than personal and nothing you caused.
Practice saying 'Hands are gentle' instead of 'no hitting' so your toddler's brain holds the correct neural image of the desired behavior.
Use a protection script when physically unsafe: 'I have to protect my body. You know I love you, but if you keep kicking me, I will move away.'
Name the feeling before correcting behavior by saying 'I see you're really frustrated that we can't have more banana - that's a big feeling.'
Practice your scripts in the mirror before a meltdown happens so the words feel natural when chaos arrives at 7 AM.
Identify your personal emotional triggers and prepare a calming strategy because children mirror nervous system regulation they observe from you.
Seek out Parent Child Interactive Therapy or a similar evidence-based program because specialized support gives you trained feedback and concrete techniques.
Bookmark four core scripts you can reference quickly because having language ready prevents fumbling during high-stress moments with an aggressive toddler.
Accept that staying calm doesn't mean being perfect - it means your toddler learns that big feelings don't have to end in aggression by watching you model it.
